plot_extraction.response_text:
Little Claus and Great Claus share an unequal arrangement in which Little Claus lends his only horse all week and receives Great Claus’s four horses on Sundays. When Little Claus boasts that all five horses are his, Great Claus kills his lone horse. Little Claus takes the hide to sell, but while seeking shelter overnight, he discovers a farmer’s wife secretly entertaining a sexton. Using the creaking hide as a supposed magical conjurer, he convinces the farmer that it has produced hidden food and wine and revealed a devil resembling the sexton. The farmer buys the “conjurer” for a bushel of money and makes Little Claus take away the chest containing the hidden sexton. Little Claus then threatens to throw the chest into a river, prompting the sexton to buy his freedom for another bushel of money.

Seeing Little Claus’s wealth and believing it came from selling the horsehide, Great Claus kills and skins all four of his horses. When he demands a bushel of money for each hide, the townspeople beat and drive him away. Seeking revenge, he tries to murder Little Claus in bed but unknowingly strikes Little Claus’s already-dead grandmother instead. Little Claus places her body in a cart and tricks a hot-tempered innkeeper into believing he has killed her, receiving another bushel of money in exchange for his silence. Great Claus then kills his own grandmother, expecting to sell her body, but terrifies an apothecary by confessing and flees empty-handed.

Enraged, Great Claus puts Little Claus in a sack and carries him toward the river to drown him. When Great Claus pauses at a church, Little Claus persuades an elderly cattle drover to take his place in the sack by claiming it will send him to heaven. Great Claus drowns the drover, while Little Claus leaves with the man’s cattle. When Great Claus later encounters Little Claus alive with the herd, Little Claus claims that underwater people gave him “sea-cattle.” Greedy Great Claus asks to be thrown into the river so he can obtain cattle too. Little Claus ties him in a sack with a heavy stone and pushes him into the water, where Great Claus sinks, leaving Little Claus to return home with the herd.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story has the style of a traditional comic folktale rendered in a plain, accessible nineteenth-century literary voice. Its narration is omniscient, linear, and strongly event-driven, opening with the formulaic “In a village there once lived” and briefly addressing the audience with “Now we shall hear what happened to them.” This creates the atmosphere of an oral storyteller recounting a supposedly “true” tale, although the events are deliberately improbable. Exposition is economical: characters are defined by a few conspicuous traits, such as Great Claus’s wealth, violence, greed, and gullibility or Little Claus’s poverty, quick wit, and opportunism. Psychological depth is limited; motives are transparent and exist chiefly to propel the next trick.

The diction is simple, concrete, and domestic, drawing on village life, farming, churchgoing, inns, trades, food, livestock, money, and household objects. Descriptions are brief but vivid, especially when they establish comfort, temptation, or danger: a “dark, gloomy forest,” a table laden with wine and roast meat, a deep and rapidly flowing river, or an imagined underwater landscape covered in flowers and grass. Evaluative adjectives such as “good,” “wicked,” “splendid,” “beautiful,” and “dreadful” give the language the direct moral colouring of a children’s tale. Archaic or period expressions—“betimes,” “wholl buy skins,” “a nights lodging,” “Heaven preserve us,” and payment by a “bushel of money”—reinforce the old-fashioned setting. The text also displays the punctuation and apostrophe irregularities of an older or imperfectly transcribed edition, with forms such as “farmers wife,” “doesnt,” “Ill,” and occasional missing spaces or malformed compounds.

Sentences are generally straightforward but often linked into long narrative chains by “and,” “but,” “so,” “then,” and “for.” This paratactic construction imitates oral storytelling and maintains rapid forward motion: one action causes another with little pause for reflection. Repeated temporal markers—“presently,” “at this moment,” “during the night,” “by sunrise,” and “as soon as”—keep the sequence easy to follow. Paragraphs frequently alternate between compact narration and direct speech. Dialogue is plainly attributed and usually serves an immediate practical purpose: issuing threats, bargaining, inventing lies, or revealing credulity. Exclamations, rhetorical questions, repetitions, and comic imperatives give it a performative quality, as in “Skins, skins!” or “Oh, no; oh, no.” Distinctive speech is less important than the recurring roles of deceiver and dupe.

Structurally, the story is cumulative and episodic. Each episode follows a similar pattern: Great Claus harms or threatens Little Claus; Little Claus converts the apparent disaster into profit through observation and deception; Great Claus imitates only the visible action, misunderstands its cause, and suffers a worse result. The dead horse leads to the “conjuror,” the dead grandmother leads to another payment, and the attempted drowning leads to the cattle trick and Great Claus’s death. Repetition with escalation supplies both coherence and comic momentum. Stock quantities and objects—the bushel of money, sack, chest, cart, hatchet, and river—function as memorable folktale devices rather than realistic details.

The prevailing tone is mischievous, matter-of-fact, and darkly comic. Violence and death are narrated with striking emotional restraint: horses and grandmothers are killed, a drover is drowned, and Great Claus sinks to the riverbed, yet the narration rarely dwells on suffering. Instead, brutality becomes part of a grotesque cause-and-effect comedy. Little Claus’s lies are treated admiringly because they represent cleverness overcoming strength and wealth, while Great Claus’s punishment seems justified by his cruelty, greed, and repeated refusal to learn. The morality is therefore folkloric rather than conventionally virtuous: cunning, adaptability, and verbal ingenuity triumph over literal-minded imitation and physical force.

Humour arises chiefly from dramatic irony and reversals of knowledge. The audience knows that the “conjuror” is only a squeaking horsehide, that the sexton is hidden in the chest, and that the grandmother is already dead, while the deceived characters interpret appearances incorrectly. Little Claus repeatedly improvises stories from information unavailable to others, turning accidents into convincing supernatural explanations. Great Claus’s extreme literalism creates the central comic pattern: he assumes that killing horses, killing a grandmother, or being thrown into a river will mechanically reproduce Little Claus’s rewards. The closing “Plump!” is an emphatic piece of sound symbolism, ending the tale with abrupt, sardonic finality.

Overall, the style combines oral-tale formulas, transparent syntax, brisk dialogue, repetition, escalating trickery, grotesque violence, and uncomplicated characterization. Its most distinctive feature is the calm narrative treatment of morally dubious ingenuity: the prose presents every deception with cheerful clarity, allowing rhythm, irony, and cumulative reversal to carry both the humour and the tale’s rough justice.

generation.response_text:
In a village there once lived two men who were both named Claus. One owned four strong horses, a broad field, a red barn, and a house with glass windows; and because he possessed so much, the villagers called him Great Claus. The other owned only one thin horse and a little cottage with a roof through which the rain sometimes fell; and therefore he was called Little Claus.

Now we shall hear what happened to them.

All the week Little Claus was obliged to lend his one horse to Great Claus, who used it with his own four at the plough. In return Great Claus lent all four of his horses to Little Claus every Sunday, for on that day no one worked in the fields, and Little Claus might drive them wherever he pleased.

This seemed a fair bargain to Great Claus, because he had five horses at work for six days and lost nothing on the seventh. Little Claus was less pleased, but he was poor, and a poor man must often accept the bargain made by a rich one.

Every Sunday morning Little Claus put on his best coat, climbed into his little cart, and drove all five horses along the road. The bells on their harness jingled splendidly, the dust rose beneath their hoofs, and Little Claus cracked his whip so loudly that every one came to the doors to look.

“Gee-up, all my horses!” he cried. “Make haste, my five beautiful horses!”

But Great Claus had warned him most particularly against saying this.

“Four of them are mine,” said Great Claus, “and you must cry, ‘Gee-up, my horse and Great Claus’s four horses!’ If you call them all your own, I shall strike your horse dead.”

Little Claus promised; but promises are soon forgotten when five horses trot merrily before a man who generally owns only one.

The next Sunday he passed the church just as the people were coming out, and he wished them to think him a very great farmer.

“Gee-up, all my horses!” he cried.

Great Claus was standing by the churchyard wall.

“Mind what you say!” he shouted. “Only one is yours.”

Little Claus nodded and drove on. But presently he met the schoolmaster, and again his heart swelled with pride.

“Gee-up, all my horses!” he called.

Great Claus had followed him and heard it.

“If you say that once more,” he said, “I shall kill your horse, as surely as I stand here.”

“Oh, no; oh, no,” replied Little Claus. “I shall remember.”

Toward evening he drove through the village again. The sun shone upon the harness, the bells rang, and several children ran beside the cart. Little Claus forgot both warning and promise.

“Gee-up, all my five horses!” he cried, cracking the whip.

Great Claus came running with a heavy wooden mallet. He struck Little Claus’s horse on the forehead, and the poor beast dropped dead between the shafts.

“There!” said Great Claus. “Now you will never again call five horses your own.”

Then he took his four horses and went home.

Little Claus stood looking at the dead animal. It had been lean and old, but it was all he had possessed, and without it he could neither plough nor carry wood.

“You have left me poorer than before,” he said, “yet perhaps the hide may be worth something.”

He skinned the horse, dried the hide as well as he could, put it into a sack, and set out for the nearest town. The road was long, and before he had travelled halfway, night overtook him in a dark, gloomy forest. The wind shook the branches, an owl cried above his head, and Little Claus could scarcely see the path.

Presently he saw a light between the trees. It came from a large farmhouse, and he went to the door and knocked.

The farmers wife opened it. She was dressed in her best gown, though it was a weekday, and the smell of roast meat came from the kitchen.

“Good evening,” said Little Claus. “Will you give a poor traveller a nights lodging? I can sleep upon the floor and ask for nothing more.”

“No,” answered the woman quickly. “My husband is away, and I will admit no stranger.”

Little Claus begged again, but she shut the door in his face.

Near the house stood a haystack, and as the night was cold, he climbed upon it and crept beneath the loose hay. From there he could see through the kitchen window.

A splendid supper had been set upon the table. There was a great roast goose, a dish of fish, white bread, cheese, cakes, and two bottles of red wine. Beside the table sat the village sexton, rubbing his hands and smiling at the farmers wife.

Little Claus had not eaten since morning, and the sight made him hungrier than ever.

“So there was no room for a poor traveller,” he whispered, “but there is room enough for the sexton and a roast goose.”

The woman filled the sextons glass.

“My husband will not return until tomorrow,” she said. “We shall have the whole evening in peace.”

At that very moment the sound of wheels came along the road.

“It is my husband!” cried the woman. “He has returned before his time. Heaven preserve us!”

She seized the food and hid it in the oven, where no fire had been lighted. She pushed the wine beneath the bench, thrust the cakes into a cupboard, and commanded the sexton to creep into a large chest in the corner.

“Be silent,” she whispered, shutting down the lid. “If he finds you here, I am undone.”

The farmer entered, wet and weary.

“What a dreadful night!” he said. “I am glad to be home. Have you nothing to eat?”

“Only porridge,” said his wife. “You were not expected until tomorrow.”

Then the farmer noticed Little Claus lying upon the haystack, for his legs stuck out from beneath the hay.

“Who is that fellow?” he asked.

“A traveller,” replied the woman. “He begged for shelter, but I sent him away.”

“That was unkind,” said the farmer. “No Christian man should sleep outdoors in such weather. Come down, friend, and share our poor supper.”

Little Claus entered the kitchen and sat at the table. The farmers wife brought a bowl of cold porridge, and the farmer ate from it without complaint; but Little Claus knew that roast goose and wine were close at hand.

The horsehide in his sack had become stiff. Whenever he moved his foot against it, it gave a dry creak.

“What have you in that sack?” asked the farmer.

“Oh, it is a conjuror,” said Little Claus.

“A conjuror?”

“Yes. He knows what is hidden in every house, and if I tread upon the sack, he speaks to me.”

Little Claus pressed the hide with his heel.

Creak! creak! went the dry skin.

“What does he say?” asked the farmer, staring.

“He says that a roast goose, a dish of fish, and several good cakes are hidden in the oven.”

The farmers wife turned pale.

“Nonsense!” she cried. “The sack is lying.”

“We shall soon know,” said her husband.

He opened the oven, and there stood the goose, the fish, the white bread, and all the rest.

“Wonderful!” exclaimed the farmer. “Why, wife, you must have prepared this as a surprise.”

“Yes, certainly,” she said. “I wished to surprise you.”

They placed the food upon the table, and Little Claus ate until he could eat no more. The farmer was delighted with the conjuror and wished to hear it speak again.

Little Claus stepped upon the sack.

Creak! creak!

“What does he say now?” asked the farmer.

“He says there are two bottles of excellent wine beneath the bench.”

The wine was found, and the farmer drank freely. Soon his cheeks were red, and he began to think Little Claus’s conjuror the most useful thing in all the world.

“Can it also show spirits?” he asked. “I should dearly like to see a devil, for I have often wondered what one looks like.”

“Yes,” replied Little Claus, “but that may be dangerous.”

“I am not afraid,” said the farmer. “Show me one!”

Little Claus pressed the hide.

Creak! creak! creak!

“The conjuror says,” he whispered, “that a devil is sitting in the chest in the corner.”

The farmers wife dropped a plate.

“In that chest?” said the farmer. “Let us open it.”

“No, no!” cried Little Claus. “The sight might kill you. Devils are dreadful creatures. Yet perhaps you may look at him through the crack, if you promise not to lift the lid.”

The farmer went to the chest and peered through a little split in the wood. Inside he saw the sextons round face, grey with fear. The sexton’s eyes rolled, and his teeth chattered.

“Heaven preserve us!” whispered the farmer. “The devil looks exactly like our sexton!”

“That is how devils deceive honest people,” said Little Claus. “They take the shape of those whom we trust.”

The farmer hurried away from the chest.

“You must sell me that conjuror,” he said. “I will give you a whole bushel of money for it.”

“A bushel!” exclaimed Little Claus. “It is worth much more. Think how it finds food and wine and discovers devils.”

“Then I will fill the bushel to the top.”

Little Claus pretended to consider. At last he sighed.

“You have treated me kindly,” he said, “and so you shall have it. But you must do me one favour. I cannot carry both the money and that heavy chest. Let me take the chest away, for I have always wanted one.”

The farmers wife quickly begged her husband to agree.

“Yes, yes,” she said. “Give him the old chest. It is of no use to us.”

The farmer filled a grain measure with silver and copper coins. Little Claus tied the money securely upon his back, loaded the chest onto a small handcart, and set off before sunrise. The farmer remained behind with the horsehide, waiting for it to tell him where more wine was hidden.

When Little Claus reached the middle of a bridge over a deep river, he stopped.

“I am tired of dragging this chest,” he said loudly. “I shall throw it into the water.”

“Do not!” cried the sexton from within. “Let me out, good friend!”

“Oh, are you still there?” said Little Claus. “I had almost forgotten.”

“Open the lid. I will give you money.”

“How much?”

“A sackful.”

“That is not enough. You are a heavy devil, and I have dragged you many miles.”

“Then a bushelful! I have money hidden near the church. Spare me, and you shall have it.”

Little Claus opened the chest, and the sexton climbed out, stiff and trembling. Together they went to a hollow tree behind the churchyard, where the sexton kept his savings. He measured out a full bushel of money, and Little Claus allowed him to run away.

Thus Little Claus returned home with two bushels of money, although he had set out with nothing but the hide of a dead horse.

When Great Claus saw so many coins, his eyes became as round as plates.

“Where did you get all that?” he asked.

“I sold my horsehide,” replied Little Claus.

“How much did they pay?”

“A bushel of money, and more besides.”

Great Claus did not stop to ask why any one would pay such a price. He ran home, took his sharpest hatchet, and killed all four of his fine horses. Then he skinned them and loaded the hides upon a cart.

“My fortune is made!” he cried. “Four hides will bring four bushels, and perhaps eight.”

He went to the town and walked through every street, shouting:

“Skins, skins! Who’ll buy skins? A bushel of money for each!”

The shoemakers laughed at him. The tanners offered a few small coins, which was the proper price, but Great Claus grew angry.

“A few coins!” he roared. “Do you take me for a fool? Little Claus received a bushel for one hide, and mine are larger and better.”

“Then sell them to the man who bought his,” said a tanner.

Great Claus continued shouting until a crowd followed him. He pushed into shops, demanded bushels of silver, and called every one a cheat. At last the townspeople lost patience. The apprentices seized broom handles, the butchers brought their switches, and the women threw cabbage stalks.

“Give him the price of his skins!” they cried.

They beat Great Claus from one end of the town to the other. His coat was torn, his hat was crushed, and he was obliged to leave the four hides lying in the mud.

“This is Little Claus’s doing,” he said as he limped home. “He has killed my horses by his wicked lies, and tonight I shall kill him.”

Little Claus had guessed that Great Claus would return in a rage. Now his old grandmother lived with him, but that very day she had died peacefully in her chair. Little Claus was sorry, for she had been good to him; yet he knew Great Claus was coming, and a clever man must use what lies before him.

He laid his grandmother in his own bed, placed his nightcap upon her head, and drew the blanket up to her chin. Then he hid beneath a pile of empty sacks in the corner.

During the night Great Claus entered with his hatchet.

“You shall not cheat me again,” he whispered.

He crept to the bed and struck the figure beneath the blanket. The old grandmother did not move.

“There,” said Great Claus. “Now you are dead.”

He went home, believing he had murdered Little Claus.

In the morning Little Claus came out from his hiding place.

“My poor grandmother,” he said. “You were dead already, but Great Claus has treated you very rudely. We must see whether his wickedness can be made to pay for your burial.”

He dressed the dead woman in her best clothes and placed her upright in a cart. He tied a cord behind her so that she would not fall, put a basket upon her arm, and drove toward the town.

At noon he reached an inn. He stopped outside and called to the innkeeper.

“My grandmother is old and deaf,” he said, “but she has money and wishes for a glass of sweet wine. Pray carry it to her while I go to the market.”

The innkeeper was a hot-tempered man. He filled a glass and took it to the cart.

“Here is your wine,” he said.

The grandmother made no reply.

“Do you hear me?” he shouted.

Still she said nothing.

The innkeeper held the glass beneath her nose.

“Pay me first, old woman.”

She remained silent and stared before her.

“Are you mocking me?” cried the innkeeper. “Do you think my wine costs nothing?”

He struck her under the chin with the back of his hand. The cord broke, and the dead grandmother fell from the cart onto the road.

At that moment Little Claus returned.

“What have you done!” he cried. “You have killed my grandmother!”

“I hardly touched her,” said the innkeeper, turning pale.

“She was alive when I left her. Look! She neither breathes nor speaks. Murder! Murder!”

“Be quiet,” begged the innkeeper. “If the magistrate hears of this, I shall be hanged.”

“You struck a poor old woman because she did not hear you.”

“I did not know she was deaf.”

“That will not bring her back.”

The innkeeper looked up and down the road. No one had seen them.

“If I give you a bushel of money, will you say she died upon the journey?”

Little Claus shook his head.

“My grandmother was worth more than that.”

“A bushel filled to the rim, and I shall also give you food for the road.”

Little Claus allowed himself to be persuaded. The innkeeper fetched his money, and Little Claus drove home with the dead grandmother and another bushel of coins.

Great Claus was watching from behind his hedge.

“What is that money?” he demanded.

“I sold my grandmother,” said Little Claus. “Dead grandmothers are fetching excellent prices in town.”

“How much?”

“One bushel of money. If the grandmother is large and well dressed, she may bring even more.”

Great Claus hurried into his house, where his own grandmother sat beside the fire knitting a stocking.

“Grandmother,” he said, “I am in need of money.”

“So are we all,” replied the old woman.

Great Claus took a mallet and struck her dead. Then he dressed her in her Sunday gown, placed her upon his back, and carried her to town.

The first shop he entered belonged to an apothecary.

“What do you want?” asked the apothecary.

“I have brought my dead grandmother,” said Great Claus. “How much will you give for her?”

The apothecary stared at him.

“Give for her?”

“Yes. She is freshly killed, and I will not accept less than a bushel of money.”

“You killed her?”

“Certainly. Do you suppose she would have died at the proper time merely to oblige me?”

The apothecary rushed to the door.

“Help! Murder! Fetch the constable!”

Great Claus was terrified. He dropped his grandmother in the shop, knocked over a shelf of bottles, and fled from the town. Dogs barked after him, boys threw stones, and the constable chased him nearly to the village.

When he reached home, breathless and empty-handed, he saw Little Claus counting his money.

“You have cheated me once too often,” he cried. “I have lost my horses, my hides, my grandmother, and nearly my liberty because of you.”

“I never told you to do any of those things,” said Little Claus.

“Silence! Tomorrow you shall be drowned.”

Great Claus seized him, thrust him into a large sack, and tied the mouth with a strong rope.

“I shall carry you to the river tonight,” he said, “and there will be no trickery this time.”

The river lay several miles away, and Little Claus was heavy, for he had eaten a good supper. Great Claus carried the sack over one shoulder, but soon his back ached and sweat ran down his face.

The road passed a church, and the organ was playing within.

“I have worked hard,” said Great Claus. “I may as well rest and hear one hymn before I drown you.”

He placed the sack beside the church wall and went inside.

Little Claus lay quietly and listened. Presently he heard the bells of cattle and the slow steps of an old man. It was a cattle drover returning from market with a fine herd of cows and oxen.

“Oh, dear! Oh, dear!” cried Little Claus from the sack. “I am too young to go to heaven! I do not wish it!”

The drover stopped.

“Who is in that sack?” he asked.

“It is I,” replied Little Claus. “I am being sent straight to heaven, but I have no desire to leave this world.”

“How can a sack send you to heaven?”

“When the church service ends, a holy man will carry the sack to the river and throw it in. Then I shall rise through the water and clouds and arrive at heavens gate before morning.”

“That is wonderful,” said the drover. “I have always wished to go to heaven, for I am old, my knees pain me, and driving cattle is wearisome.”

“You may take my place if you like.”

“Will it truly send me there?”

“Certainly. But you must remain very quiet. If you cry out, the holy man may think you unworthy.”

The drover untied the sack, and Little Claus climbed out.

“Quickly,” said Little Claus. “The hymn is nearly finished.”

The old man crept into the sack, and Little Claus tied it securely. Then he took the drovers staff and drove the cattle away by a path behind the church.

Presently Great Claus came out. He lifted the sack and was surprised at its weight.

“You have grown heavier,” he said.

The old drover remembered that he must remain silent.

Great Claus carried him to the river. The night was black, and the water ran deep and rapidly between steep banks.

“You cheated me with the hide,” said Great Claus, “and with the grandmother, but you shall cheat me no more. Into the river you go!”

The drover said nothing.

Great Claus swung the sack once, twice, three times, and threw it far into the stream.

Splash!

The sack disappeared beneath the dark water.

“There,” said Great Claus. “Now Little Claus is at the bottom, and I shall live in peace.”

He walked home and slept soundly.

The next morning he went to his field, though he had no horses left to plough it. As he stood by the gate, he heard the lowing of cattle. Along the road came Little Claus, driving a splendid herd. There were red cows, black cows, white oxen, spotted calves, and a great bull with a brass ring in its nose.

“Good morning, Great Claus!” he called.

Great Claus turned as pale as flour.

“Were you not drowned last night?”

“Oh yes,” replied Little Claus. “You threw me into the deepest part of the river.”

“Then how have you returned?”

“The river people released me.”

“What river people?”

“Why, those who live beneath the water. There are whole villages down there, with church towers, houses, gardens, and meadows. The grass is greener than any grass upon earth, and the flowers shine like silver. These cattle came from the river meadows.”

Great Claus looked greedily at the herd.

“Were they given to you?”

“Yes, though I received only a small number because you threw me too near the bank. Had I fallen into the deepest place, I should have found thousands.”

“Thousands of cattle?”

“Certainly. The bottom is covered with them. Sea-cattle have broad backs, rich milk, and horns that never break. I was told to return tomorrow for another herd, but I hardly have room for these.”

Great Claus walked around the cattle and examined them. They were fat and healthy, and the bell on the leading cow was made of good bronze.

“How does one reach this underwater country?” he asked.

“One must be tied in a sack and thrown into the river. Otherwise the current carries a man away before the river people can find him.”

Great Claus considered. He had no horses, no money, and no grandmother, but if he owned a thousand sea-cattle, he would be the richest farmer in the district.

“You must take me there at once,” he said.

“I am busy,” replied Little Claus. “These cattle need feeding.”

“I shall give you half of those I bring back.”

“No. The journey is dangerous.”

“Then you may keep one hundred.”

Little Claus shook his head.

“Two hundred!”

“I do not know.”

“Five hundred!” cried Great Claus. “Only tie me in the sack and throw me into the deepest place.”

“Well,” said Little Claus, “as you ask it so earnestly, I shall do my best.”

They went to Great Claus’s barn and found the same large sack. Great Claus climbed inside, but before Little Claus tied it, he said, “We must take a heavy stone.”

“What for?” asked Great Claus.

“To make certain that you sink quickly. Yesterday I went down slowly and nearly missed the finest meadows.”

“Then choose the heaviest stone you can carry.”

Little Claus rolled a great stone into the bottom of the sack. Great Claus squeezed in beside it, though there was hardly room.

“It is uncomfortable,” he said.

“The road to riches is not always soft,” replied Little Claus.

He tied the sack with two ropes, placed it upon a cart, and drove toward the river. The cattle followed behind, their bells ringing.

As they approached the bridge, Great Claus called from the sack, “Are we nearly there?”

“Yes.”

“Remember the deepest place!”

“I shall.”

“And if you see me rising, push me under again, or I may lose the thousand cattle.”

“I shall remember that also.”

At the middle of the bridge Little Claus stopped the cart. The river roared below, swollen by rain, and white foam curled around the rocks.

“This is the place,” he said.

“Are you certain it is deep?”

“No one has ever found the bottom.”

“Excellent! Throw me in.”

Little Claus dragged the sack to the edge.

“Do not forget,” cried Great Claus. “A thousand cattle, perhaps two thousand!”

“You were always fond of having more than other people,” said Little Claus.

He tipped the sack over the edge.

Down it fell, struck the water, and vanished.

Plump!

For one moment a few bubbles rose to the surface; then the current swept them away. The heavy stone carried Great Claus to the muddy bottom, and neither the river people nor the sea-cattle came to meet him.

Little Claus stood upon the bridge and looked at the water.

“You killed my horse because I called five horses mine,” he said, “and you tried to kill me because you could not learn that another mans good fortune cannot be copied with a hatchet. Now the river may teach you, though I fear you are a poor scholar.”

Then he drove the cattle home.

With part of the money he repaired his cottage and gave his grandmother a proper burial. With the rest he bought fields, a warm stable, and a cart painted blue. He cared well for the herd, and before many years had passed he possessed more cattle than Great Claus had ever dreamed of owning.

Whenever Little Claus drove through the village, the children ran after him, and the bells rang merrily upon the harness. Yet he no longer cried that every horse and cow was his, for he had learned that boasting may cost a man dearly, even when his wit afterwards repays him.

As for the villagers, they often spoke of Great Claus and wondered how a man who had owned four horses, a broad field, and a red barn had lost everything.

“He was strong,” said one.

“He was rich,” said another.

“But he was greedy,” said a third, “and greed can put a heavier stone in a sack than any man can lift.”

And that was the truest word of all.

# The Lighthouse at the End of the Road

When Mara Venn returned to Bellwether, the sea was missing.

She noticed it before she noticed anything else. The road from the railway station climbed the black cliffs in seven familiar turns, and on the fourth, where the pines opened and the horizon had always appeared, there was only white.

Not mist. Not cloud. White—flat, depthless, absolute.

The carriage driver refused to look at it.

“Bad weather,” he said, though the November sky above them was blue.

Mara leaned toward the window. Far below, the cliffs descended into that blankness. There was no sound of waves, no gulls circling over the water, no dark line dividing sea from sky. Bellwether had been built around the ocean: its crooked houses faced it, its streets tilted toward it, its people slept to its breathing. Yet now the town seemed perched above an unfinished page.

“How long has it been like this?” she asked.

The driver flicked the reins. “Like what?”

Mara studied the back of his wool cap. “The sea.”

His shoulders tightened.

“There’s never been a sea here, Miss Venn.”

He said it gently, as one speaks to the recently bereaved.

Mara sat back.

She had been away twelve years. Long enough for roofs to sag, children to become adults, and grudges to soften into stories. Not long enough for an ocean to vanish.

The carriage stopped outside the house where she had grown up. It was smaller than she remembered, with gray boards and green shutters. Her mother’s brass wind chimes still hung above the porch, perfectly still.

Mr. Sallow, the family solicitor, waited by the gate. He was a thin man in a coat too large for him, and he twisted his hat in his hands.

“My condolences,” he said. “Your father was an important man.”

“He kept a lighthouse.”

“Just so.”

“Did anyone find him?”

Mr. Sallow looked past her, toward the white beyond the cliffs. “No.”

Mara paid the driver and carried her valise inside.

The house smelled of dust, salt, and lamp oil.

At least, she thought it smelled of salt. When she mentioned this, Mr. Sallow gave her the same concerned look as the driver.

They sat at the kitchen table. The blue cup her father had used every morning stood beside the cold stove. A brown ring had dried at its bottom.

“He left a will,” said Mr. Sallow, drawing papers from his case. “The house is yours. His savings as well, though they are modest. And the tower.”

“The lighthouse?”

“The tower,” he corrected. “On North Point.”

“What happened to him?”

“No one knows. Three weeks ago, he failed to come into town for supplies. Mr. Pike went to check on him. The lamp was burning, but your father was gone.”

“Was the door locked?”

“Yes.”

“From the inside?”

“Yes.”

“And the windows?”

“Also locked.”

Mara looked through the kitchen window. Beyond the garden, the land sloped toward North Point. The lighthouse stood there, slender and white, its glass crown shining in the afternoon sun.

“Then how did Mr. Pike get in?”

Mr. Sallow hesitated. “He had a key.”

“Who else has one?”

“Only you, now.”

He placed a long iron key on the table.

Mara touched it. It was warm.

Mr. Sallow cleared his throat. “There is one other matter. Your father left a letter with me. He instructed me to give it to you if he disappeared.”

“Not if he died?”

“He was specific.”

The envelope bore her name in her father’s square handwriting. Mara opened it with her thumb.

Inside was a single sheet.

Mara,

The town will tell you there is no sea. The town is wrong.

Light the lamp before the seventh night.

Do not let them stop you.

Forgive me.

Father

She read it twice.

“What does he mean?” she asked.

But Mr. Sallow had risen from his chair.

“I wouldn’t know.”

“You knew my father for thirty years.”

“And for thirty years, Orin Venn said many things I did not understand.” He fastened his case. “If I may offer advice, Miss Venn: sell the house, forget the tower, and return to wherever you have made your life.”

“Kingsport.”

“Yes. Return to Kingsport.”

“Why?”

He glanced at the envelope.

“Because tomorrow will be your second day.”

Before Mara could question him, he left.

That night, she dreamed of drowning.

She stood at the bottom of the sea, though no water surrounded her. Fish moved through the white in silver flashes. Above her, the lighthouse beam turned in slow circles, illuminating a ceiling of waves. Her father was climbing toward her along the beam as if it were a staircase.

His hair was white now. His face looked older than it had in the photograph on her desk in Kingsport.

“Mara,” he called.

She tried to answer, but seawater filled her mouth.

She woke before dawn with her bedclothes soaked in cold brine.

By breakfast, they were dry.

Mara went into town.

Bellwether had one main street, one church, two public houses, and an excessive number of clocks. Clocks hung in shop windows and over doorways. The town hall clock rose above the square. Even the church steeple had a round black face beneath its cross.

Every clock showed six minutes past three.

People recognized Mara. She saw it in the way conversations stopped when she passed. Yet few greeted her. Mrs. Pike, who had once given Mara sugared buns after school, turned her bakery sign from OPEN to CLOSED as Mara approached.

Only Theo Vale seemed glad to see her.

He came out of the chandlery carrying a coil of rope over one shoulder. He had been a long-limbed, solemn boy when Mara left. Now he was broad and sun-browned, though there was no sun on the white expanse below the cliffs.

“You came,” he said.

“You sound surprised.”

“I hoped you wouldn’t.”

He smiled, but the smile did not reach his eyes.

They embraced awkwardly. Mara remembered racing him barefoot over the rocks, stealing apples from the vicar’s garden, and once, when they were fifteen, kissing him behind her father’s oil shed. The memories felt more vivid than the man before her.

“Theo,” she said, “where is the sea?”

His face emptied.

“There’s never been a sea here.”

She slapped him.

The sound cracked across the square. A dozen townspeople pretended not to watch.

Theo touched his cheek. Then, almost imperceptibly, he nodded.

“Good,” he whispered.

Mara stared.

“Come to the old net house after dark,” he said aloud. “We can discuss your father’s accounts.”

“I didn’t ask about—”

“After dark.”

He walked away without looking back.

Mara spent the afternoon at the lighthouse.

The path to North Point was overgrown with sea lavender. Tiny purple flowers brushed her skirts, releasing a smell like rain. The tower’s red door stood beneath a stone lintel carved with the year 1791.

Her key turned easily.

Inside, nothing suggested a struggle. Her father’s boots waited by the door. A kettle sat on the stove. His bed was neatly made. On a shelf lay forty-three journals, each labeled by year.

Mara opened the newest.

October 3. Lamp lit at sunset. White perimeter advanced seven yards.

October 4. Mrs. Pike no longer recalls her eldest son. She believes she has only two daughters. Thomas Pike’s name remains in the harbor register.

October 6. Bell tower stopped at 3:06. Repaired it. Stopped again.

October 9. Dreamed of Elian. Heard him knocking below the foundations.

Mara paused.

Elian was her brother.

He had drowned when she was eight and he was eleven. He had gone out in their father’s small boat during a sudden storm. They found the boat split against the rocks, but they never found his body.

She turned the page.

October 12. White reached the harbor mouth.

October 13. Harbor gone. Town remembers quarry in its place.

October 15. Could not light the lamp. Wicks damp though stores are dry.

October 16. Sea no longer visible from lantern room.

October 18. Mara must not come. I wrote to her telling her to stay away.

October 19. Burned the letter.

October 21. I am forgetting Elian’s voice.

October 22. There has never been a sea here.

The final sentence had been scratched out so violently that the nib tore the paper.

Below it, her father had written:

That is how it enters.

Mara climbed the spiral stairs.

At the top, the lamp waited inside the glass lantern room. Its great lens surrounded the central burner like a crystal hive. The fuel reservoir was full. The brass had been polished. Everything was ready.

She struck a match.

Before the flame touched the wick, the lantern-room door flew open behind her.

Mara spun around.

Three men stood on the stairs: Mayor Quill, Constable Rusk, and Mr. Sallow.

The mayor removed his hat. He had grown heavy since Mara last saw him, but his eyes remained small and bright.

“You cannot light that,” he said.

“Why?”

“It disturbs people.”

“It’s a lighthouse.”

“It is an obsolete tower on an empty cliff.”

Mara held the match until it burned her fingers. She dropped it with a curse.

Mr. Sallow would not meet her gaze.

“My father believed the light kept something away.”

“Your father was ill,” said Mayor Quill.

“Then why are you frightened?”

Constable Rusk stepped forward. “Come down, Miss Venn.”

Mara rested one hand on the lamp.

The constable stopped.

For a moment no one moved.

Then, from somewhere far beneath them, came a sound.

Knock.

Knock.

Knock.

It seemed to rise through the tower’s stones.

Mayor Quill went pale. Mr. Sallow closed his eyes.

“What is that?” Mara asked.

“Foundation settling,” said the mayor.

Knock.

Knock.

Knock.

A drop of seawater fell from the ceiling and struck the lamp’s brass housing.

Mayor Quill backed toward the stairs. “You have until tomorrow to leave Bellwether. The tower will be sealed.”

They descended quickly. Mr. Sallow lingered just long enough to whisper, “Tonight is your second night.”

Then he followed.

At midnight, Mara went to the net house.

It stood behind the abandoned customs office, though everyone in town insisted the building had once stored mining equipment. Theo waited inside beside a hooded lantern.

“You hit harder than you did at fifteen,” he said.

“You deserved it.”

“I did.”

Old nets hung from the rafters, stiff with salt. Theo pulled aside a stack of rotting lobster pots and revealed a trapdoor.

Below was a cellar filled with contraband memories.

There were oars, sextants, shells, bottles of sand, children’s toy boats, and paintings of ships. Shelves bowed beneath harbor records. A whale’s rib hung on one wall, longer than Mara was tall.

“My mother started hiding things when people began forgetting,” Theo said. “She could feel memories slipping. Objects help.”

“Why did you lie to me?”

“Because saying the truth in daylight makes it hear you.”

“What is it?”

Theo looked toward the ceiling.

“We call it the Pale.”

Mara remembered the flat white horizon.

Theo continued. “No one knows what it is. Your father thought it lived beneath the sea, or outside the world, and the lighthouse kept it from reaching shore. Not the flame itself—the turning beam. A circle drawn over and over. A boundary.”

“Why hasn’t anyone lit the lamp since he vanished?”

“The mayor forbade it.”

“Why?”

“Because the light brings back what the Pale has taken.”

“That sounds like a reason to light it.”

“Not everything taken was loved.”

Theo lifted the lantern hood.

On a table lay a child’s red mitten.

Mara knew it. Elian had worn the pair the winter before he drowned.

She picked it up with trembling fingers.

“The Pale doesn’t simply erase things,” Theo said. “It takes pain first. Then whatever caused the pain. Then everything connected to it.”

“Elian.”

“After he drowned, your father kept the lighthouse burning every night. But years later, when the old mechanism broke and the lamp stopped for three days, people forgot the worst things that had happened to them. Mayor Quill forgot his wife’s death. Mrs. Pike forgot her son, who was lost in a storm. My mother forgot the fire that scarred her. They felt relieved.”

“And they let it continue.”

“Some did. At first.”

Theo moved the lantern across the cellar. Its light revealed labels tied to objects.

HARBOR.

GULLS.

TIDES.

THE ISLAND OF SAINT ORRA.

SUMMER REGATTA, 1902.

“By the time they understood the price,” he said, “they had forgotten enough to doubt there was a price at all.”

Mara thought of the frozen clocks.

“Why does Mr. Sallow keep counting my days?”

“The Pale works slowly on strangers. Seven nights, your father believed. On the first, you dream of the lost. On the second, you doubt. On the third, familiar names sound strange. By the seventh, you belong to the white.”

“What happens then?”

“You stop noticing what disappears.”

A bell rang somewhere outside.

Three slow notes.

Theo lowered the lantern hood.

“The church clock hasn’t rung in weeks,” he said.

They climbed from the cellar.

In the square, every door stood open.

Townspeople emerged in silence, wearing nightclothes beneath their coats. Men, women, and children turned toward North Point.

The lighthouse was shining.

A pale beam swept across the town.

As it touched the first row of houses, people screamed.

Mrs. Pike fell to her knees. “Thomas,” she cried. “Oh, God. Thomas.”

Mayor Quill staggered against the fountain, calling his wife’s name.

The beam crossed Mara.

Memory struck like lightning.

Elian laughing with a gap between his front teeth. Elian pushing her into a tide pool. Elian at the kitchen table, drawing sea monsters in the margins of Father’s charts. Elian on the morning of the storm, furious and tear-streaked.

You told him, a voice whispered inside her.

Mara remembered.

She had broken their father’s compass while playing with it. Afraid of punishment, she blamed Elian. Their father believed her and struck him. Elian ran from the house, took the boat, and sailed into the storm.

Mara sank to the cobblestones.

The lighthouse beam moved on. Its glow vanished, but the memory remained.

“I killed him,” she said.

Theo knelt beside her. “You were a child.”

“I lied.”

“You didn’t summon the storm.”

“I let Father blame him.”

Across the square, Mayor Quill roared, “Put it out!”

Constable Rusk and several others ran toward North Point.

“Who lit it?” Mara asked.

Theo looked at the tower. “Maybe your father.”

They followed.

The lighthouse door stood open. Inside, wet footprints crossed the floor—bare human prints leading toward the stairs.

Mara and Theo climbed past townspeople descending in terror. Some wept. Some clawed at their own faces. The turning light restored shipwrecks, betrayals, graves, and names long erased. Bellwether remembered itself all at once.

At the lantern room, they found Mr. Sallow chained to the lamp mechanism.

He had wrapped the iron links around his waist and fastened them with a padlock so no one could drag him away. Blood ran from a cut above his eye. The great lens turned behind him.

“I was a coward,” he said when he saw Mara. “For three weeks.”

“Where is my father?”

Sallow pointed downward.

“The foundation.”

The knocking came again.

Not three knocks now, but hundreds.

Mara descended to the bottom floor. Theo found an iron ring beneath her father’s bed. Together they pulled, revealing a narrow stone stairway spiraling underground.

Cold air rushed up, smelling of deep water.

They carried a lamp down.

The staircase ended in a cavern beneath the cliffs. Black rock arched overhead. At the center stood a pool as smooth as glass.

The missing sea was inside it.

Mara saw moonlit waves beneath the surface, stretching downward into impossible distance. Ships sailed upside down. Gulls wheeled in a submerged sky. Entire islands floated in the depths.

And her father stood on the water.

He looked thin and exhausted. White strands moved through his hair like smoke.

“Mara,” he said.

She stepped toward him, but Theo caught her arm.

“Don’t touch the pool.”

Her father smiled sadly. “He always was sensible.”

“Come back,” Mara said.

“I can’t.”

“What happened?”

“I tried to bargain.”

The surface around his boots rippled. Faces appeared beneath it, thousands of them, their mouths open.

“The Pale offered Elian to me,” he said. “Not a ghost. Not a memory. Elian alive, untouched by the storm. It said it would return him if I extinguished the lamp.”

“You believed it?”

“I wanted to.”

Above them, the lighthouse mechanism groaned. The beam continued turning, and with each revolution the cavern shook.

“When I put out the light,” her father said, “the Pale came through. But it did not return your brother. It only returned my guilt.”

Mara swallowed. “Then come away from it.”

“I am holding the door closed.”

She looked closer. The white strands were not in his hair. They passed through him, thin as threads, binding his body to the pool.

The lantern flame flickered.

Behind her father, something vast moved under the inverted sea.

The white horizon had never been emptiness. It was an eye pressed against the world.

“Mara,” her father said, “the lamp will not be enough now. The Pale has crossed too far. The boundary must be redrawn from here.”

“How?”

“Someone must carry the light into the pool.”

Theo’s grip tightened. “No.”

“The lens above gathers memory,” Orin said. “Joy and grief alike. The light must be brought below before sunrise.”

“Then you do it,” Theo said.

“I am already mostly forgotten. The light needs someone the town remembers.”

Mara laughed once, bitterly. “They barely remember me.”

“The town does not,” said her father. “But you remember yourself.”

The cavern trembled again. Cracks raced across the ceiling.

From above came a metallic crash.

The beam stopped turning.

Darkness thickened around the pool.

Theo lifted the lantern. “That’s all we have.”

It was a small oil lamp, hardly brighter than a candle.

Mara thought of the great lens overhead, no longer gathering the restored memories of Bellwether. She thought of townspeople trying to destroy it, preferring peaceful emptiness to unbearable truth.

Then she thought of Elian’s red mitten.

“Keep this burning,” she told Theo.

“Mara—”

“If the light needs memory, give it one.”

She took the lamp from him and faced the pool.

Her father shook his head. “You do not owe me this.”

“No,” she said. “I don’t.”

The Pale surged upward. White spread across the pool, swallowing ships, stars, and drowned faces.

Mara held the lamp against her chest.

She remembered Elian on the cliff path, his red mittens bright against the snow. She remembered him breaking his biscuit in half because she had dropped hers. She remembered the compass, the lie, their father’s anger, and the boat vanishing into rain.

She did not push the guilt away.

She made room beside it for love.

The lamp blazed.

Its light changed from gold to blue, then to the silver of moonlight on water.

Mara stepped onto the pool.

Cold pierced her shoes. Beneath her feet, the sea opened like a sky.

The Pale spoke without words.

It promised relief.

It showed her a life in which Elian had never existed, and therefore had never died. Her father had never struck him. Mara had never lied. There was no guilt, no grief, no storm.

In that life, Mara felt almost nothing.

She took another step.

The white rose to her knees. Names slipped from her mind: Mrs. Pike. Mr. Sallow. Theo.

She looked back.

A man stood at the pool’s edge, shouting something. She knew his face mattered, though his name was gone.

Ahead, her father was fading.

Mara raised the lamp.

“My brother was Elian Venn,” she said.

The white recoiled.

“He was eleven years old. He hated onions. He could swim farther than anyone in Bellwether. He drew monsters on maps.”

The lamp brightened.

“My father is Orin Venn. He kept the lighthouse. He failed us, and he loved us.”

The pool cracked from shore to shore.

“My name is Mara.”

Light poured through the cracks.

The Pale screamed.

The sound was the roar of every wave Bellwether had forgotten.

Water exploded upward. Theo dragged Mara back as the cavern filled with wind and salt spray. Her father stood at the center of the storm, smiling.

For one instant, another boy appeared beside him, wearing red mittens.

Then the sea turned itself right side up.

At dawn, Bellwether woke to gulls.

The ocean had returned below the cliffs, gray and restless beneath the morning sky. Boats lay stranded in streets where people had built houses over the forgotten harbor. Fish glittered in flooded cellars. The town’s clocks began to strike, each choosing a different hour.

The lighthouse was dark.

They found Mara on the rocks at North Point, clinging to Theo’s hand. They found no trace of Orin Venn.

For seven days, the people of Bellwether remembered.

They remembered their dead and the ways they had failed them. They remembered storms, fires, cruel words, and doors closed when they should have opened. Some packed their belongings and left. Some stayed and repaired the harbor. Mrs. Pike placed a stone for Thomas beside the graves of her daughters.

Mayor Quill resigned.

Mr. Sallow slept for two days, woke, and began setting the town records in order.

On the eighth night, Mara climbed the lighthouse stairs.

The great lens was cracked, and the mechanism groaned, but Theo had repaired enough of it to turn. Together they filled the reservoir and trimmed the wick.

“Do you think it will come back?” he asked.

Mara looked through the glass.

The sea stretched to the horizon, dark and full of weather. Somewhere beneath it lay all the things people wished to forget.

“Yes,” she said. “Not tonight, perhaps. But someday.”

“Then we’ll keep the lamp burning.”

“We?”

Theo smiled. “You’ll need someone sensible.”

Mara lit the wick.

The beam swept over Bellwether, touching roofs, streets, gravestones, and faces. People paused as it passed, remembering what they had lost.

Some wept.

Some smiled.

Out at sea, the light drew a bright circle across the waves, and for a moment Mara saw two figures standing beyond the breakers: a man and a boy, hand in hand.

Then the beam moved on.

The figures vanished, but the sea remained.
